title: Rate limiting
summary: Why services limit request rates, the common algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket), where to enforce it, and distributed rate limiting with a shared store.
note:
1. Why: protect capacity, stop abuse, enforce fair-use/quotas
2. Algorithms
   • Fixed window: count per clock window — simple, bursty at edges
   • Sliding window: smooths the edge boundary
   • Token bucket: refill tokens at a rate, allow bursts up to capacity
   • Leaky bucket: process at a steady rate, queue/drop overflow
3. Enforce at the edge (gateway/LB); share state in Redis so all nodes agree
4. Respond 429 with Retry-After
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.a: Token bucket refills tokens at a rate and allows bursts up to capacity; leaky bucket drains at a fixed steady rate and smooths/queues bursts.
A client can spend its full quota at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, allowing ~2× the limit across the boundary.

recall.q: Why does distributed rate limiting need a shared store?
recall.a: Counts must be consistent across all servers, so a shared store like Redis holds the per-key counter instead of per-node memory.

shot.title: Algorithm trade-offs
shot.body:
| algorithm | bursts | memory | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| fixed window | edge spikes | tiny | simplest |
| sliding window | smoother | moderate | fixes edge |
| token bucket | allowed up to cap | small | common default |
| leaky bucket | smoothed out | small | steady output |

sections.title: Why rate limit
sections.body: ✍️ Limiting request rate protects backend capacity from overload, blunts abuse (scraping, brute force, DDoS), and enforces fair-use quotas and paid tiers. The usual response is HTTP **429 Too Many Requests** with a `Retry-After` header.

sections.title: Fixed and sliding window
sections.body:
✍️ **Fixed window:** count requests per clock interval (e.g. per minute); reset at the boundary. Simple but lets a client burst at the end of one window and start of the next (~2× the limit).
✍️ **Sliding window:** count over a moving interval (log of timestamps or a weighted blend of the current and previous window) to smooth that edge.

sections.title: Token and leaky bucket
sections.body:
✍️ **Token bucket:** tokens refill at a steady rate up to a capacity; each request spends one; an empty bucket rejects. Allows controlled bursts — the common default.
✍️ **Leaky bucket:** requests enter a fixed-size queue drained at a constant rate; overflow is dropped. Produces a smooth, steady output.
```java
boolean allow(String key) {           // token bucket sketch
    Bucket b = buckets.get(key);
    b.refill();                       // add tokens by elapsed time
    return b.tokens-- > 0;            // reject when empty → 429
}
```

sections.title: Distributed rate limiting
sections.body:
✍️ With many app servers, per-node counters undercount the real total. Enforce at the **edge** (API gateway / LB) and keep counters in a **shared store** like Redis using atomic ops (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`, or a Lua token-bucket script) so every node sees the same count.
- Trade-off: a central store adds a network hop and is itself a dependency to make highly available.
